title: Nothing gained (section 22)
hookLine: in the highest awakening, not even the least thing is gained

lines: WHAT DID YOU GET OUT OF IT?
cards: So, what did you get out of it? It's a question that follows people home from all sorts of things: a weekend away, a class, a hard year, a long talk with a friend.
We want to point at something we're carrying back, a skill, a lesson, a photo, a certificate.
Section twenty-two of the Diamond Sutra puts that question to the Buddha's own awakening, and the answer, in his own words, is startling.

teach.b: First, the size. Section twenty-two is only a few lines long. No sands of the Ganges, no worlds of treasure, just a question and an answer, like the moment in a long conversation when someone finally says the plain thing.

When you reached the highest, most complete awakening, Subhuti asks, was it that you reached nothing? He isn't being cheeky. He's been listening all through this sutra, and he's drawing the line out to its end.

teach.h: SO IT IS, SO IT IS.
teach.b: So it is, Subhuti, so it is, the Buddha says, the words doubled as if to make sure nobody softens them.
In that highest awakening, not even the least thing is found or gained, and that is what is called the highest, most complete awakening.
The Sanskrit is anuttara samyak sambodhi: awakening with nothing above it, whole and right. Its wholeness, the sutra claims, comes from there being nothing in it to hold. Fourth, an ordinary day.
If awakening isn't a thing acquired, it can't be stacked on a shelf with other accomplishments, or lost, or compared.
One way to picture it: less like buying a lamp, more like opening the curtains. The light was never something you owned. What changes is what's no longer in the way.
This doesn't make practice pointless. The Buddha practiced, and the sutra keeps urging people to keep and recite it. It only means practice isn't a purchase.
You can work hard at something and still not need to walk away holding it.

how: In some Zen teaching, practice is described as sitting without a gaining mind, not trying to acquire anything; section 22 is read as supporting this.

o: awakening is a prize you finally win after long effort
practice is pointless, so there's no reason to try
in the highest awakening, not even the least thing is gained

games.q: not the least thing: tap the pairs.

s: section 22 is one of the long sections of the sutra
it's only a few lines: one question and one answer.
the Buddha says not even the least thing is gained in the highest awakening
and that, he says, is what is called the highest awakening.
the sutra says that since nothing is gained, practice is pointless
it keeps urging people to keep and recite it; practice just isn't a purchase.

games.q: Subhuti asks the Buddha: when you reached the highest awakening, was it that you reached nothing? what does the Buddha say?
o: so it is, so it is
games.why: he agrees, twice: not even the least thing is gained, and that is called the highest awakening.

practice: Notice what you're hoping to get out of these two minutes, calm, insight, a better mood, a streak kept, and name it quietly.

Then set it down like a bag on the floor beside you, and sit without needing to get anything; if the hope comes back, name it and set it down again. Let the breath come and go, gaining nothing, losing nothing.

wordCard.voice: Nothing gained. Section twenty-two says that in the highest awakening, not even the least thing is gained, and that is called awakening. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: awakening; in anuttara samyak sambodhi, the highest, most complete awakening.

carryVoice: Your line: not the least thing. Curtains open, nothing bought. Back tomorrow, same hill.
